title: FROM FUGITIVE TO DELIVERER
paragraphs: FROM FUGITIVE TO DELIVERER
The desert does not ask how you got there.
It does not care whether you arrived because of your own mistakes, someone else's betrayal, or circumstances beyond your control.
It simply swallows your plans, strips away your titles, and leaves you alone with yourself.
Moses knew that feeling.
Long before he became one of the most influential figures in redemptive history, before seas split, before plagues fell upon Egypt, before a nation followed him toward freedom, Moses was a fugitive.
A wanted man.
A murderer.
A failure hiding in the wilderness.
And perhaps that is exactly why his story still reaches into modern hearts with such force.
Because many people know what it feels like to run.
Not always from the law.
But from shame.
From regret.
From disappointment.
From the wreckage of who they thought they would become.
The story of Moses is not ultimately about a hero rising to greatness.
It is about how God finds broken people in forgotten places and rewrites everything.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The story begins in oppression.
The descendants of Abraham had multiplied greatly in Egypt. What began as a refuge during Joseph's lifetime had become a place of bondage. Pharaoh feared their growing numbers and enslaved them.
Into this darkness a child was born.
His Hebrew name was מֹשֶׁה (Mosheh).
The name is traditionally connected with the Hebrew verb מָשָׁה (mashah), meaning "to draw out," reflecting Pharaoh's daughter's words:
"I drew him out of the water" (Exodus 2:10).
Even before Moses understood his purpose, God had embedded a prophecy within his name.
He would become the man through whom God would draw an entire nation out of slavery.
Yet purpose does not prevent pain.
Calling does not eliminate struggle.
Anointing does not guarantee immediate maturity.
Raised within Pharaoh's household, Moses lived between two worlds. He possessed the privileges of Egyptian royalty while carrying the bloodline of Israel.
He belonged everywhere.
And nowhere.
Many readers understand that tension.
The struggle of identity.
The feeling of never fully fitting into any category.
The loneliness of living between expectations.
One day Moses witnessed an Egyptian beating a Hebrew slave.
Something exploded inside him.
The text says he looked both ways before acting (Exodus 2:12).
Then he killed the Egyptian and buried the body.
It was impulsive.
Violent.
Sinful.
And devastating.
The man who would one day deliver Israel attempted to accomplish God's work through human anger.
The result was disaster.
When Pharaoh learned what happened, Moses fled.
Everything changed overnight.
The palace became a memory.
The future collapsed.
The prince became a fugitive.
Acts 7:29 records that Moses fled into Midian.
For forty years.
Not forty days.
Not forty weeks.
Forty years.
Imagine carrying failure for four decades.
Imagine waking every morning wondering whether your best opportunity had already passed.
Imagine believing that the defining moment of your life would forever be your greatest mistake.
Many people live there emotionally.
A failed marriage.
A ruined relationship.
A moral collapse.
An addiction.
A betrayal.
A decision they would undo if they could.
The years pass, but the guilt remains.
Yet Scripture repeatedly reveals a truth the world often misses:
God is not limited by the chapters that seem to define us.
What appears final to us is often preparation to Him.
Then came the fire.
Exodus 3 describes one of the most astonishing encounters in Scripture.
A bush burned but was not consumed.
When Moses approached, God called his name.
"Moses, Moses."
The repetition carries profound significance.
In Hebrew thought, repeating a name communicates intimacy, urgency, and affection.
This was not merely information.
This was invitation.
The fugitive discovered he had not been forgotten.
The Hebrew text records God's declaration:
אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה
Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh.
Commonly translated:
"I AM WHO I AM."
(Exodus 3:14)
The phrase carries layers of meaning that exceed any single English rendering.
It communicates God's eternal self-existence, His unchanging nature, His absolute sovereignty, and His covenant faithfulness.
The God speaking from the fire was not reacting to history.
He was governing it.
Not even Moses' failures had escaped His authority.
This moment reveals something remarkable.
God did not begin by discussing Moses' past.
He spoke about His presence.
The focus was not:
"Moses, let's revisit every mistake you've made."
The focus was:
"Certainly I will be with you" (Exodus 3:12).
That remains God's answer to fearful hearts.
His presence is greater than our past.
Moses immediately objected.
Who am I?
What if they do not believe me?
What if I cannot speak?
What if I fail?
Again.
His insecurities sound surprisingly modern.
Beneath every excuse was one fear:
Can God really use someone like me?
The answer echoes throughout Scripture.
Yes.
Not because human weakness becomes strength.
But because divine grace transforms weakness into a platform for God's glory.
The Apostle Paul would later write:
(2 Corinthians 12:10)
God specializes in using people who know they need Him.
Moses eventually returned to Egypt.
Not as a prince.
Not as a celebrity.
Not as a military conqueror.
But as a servant carrying God's word.
Again and again he stood before Pharaoh with a simple message:
"שַׁלַּח אֶת־עַמִּי"
Shallach et-ammi.
"Let My people go."
(Exodus 5:1)
The phrase became one of history's greatest declarations of freedom.
What makes it remarkable is not merely the command itself.
It is who delivered it.
A former fugitive.
A man who once ran away.
A man who believed his story was over.
A man whose greatest failure became part of God's greater redemption.
The Exodus itself ultimately points beyond Moses.
The entire story serves as a shadow of a greater Deliverer.
The New Testament repeatedly presents Jesus as the fulfillment of themes established in Exodus.
Israel was enslaved.
Humanity is enslaved to sin.
Israel needed rescue.
Humanity needs redemption.
Israel required a deliverer.
Humanity requires a Savior.
The Greek New Testament uses the word σωτήρ (sōtēr), meaning "Savior" or "Deliverer."
Jesus is not merely a teacher of morality.
He is the Deliverer Moses foreshadowed.
Where Moses led people through the sea, Christ leads people through death into life.
Where Moses mediated a covenant, Christ established the New Covenant through His blood.
Where Moses delivered from earthly bondage, Jesus delivers from eternal separation from God.
This is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
It is not fundamentally about good people becoming better.
It is about dead people being made alive.
It is about rebels becoming children.
It is about fugitives becoming family.
Perhaps that is why Moses' story continues to resonate so deeply.
Because countless people secretly identify more with the fugitive than the deliverer.
They know the hidden mistakes.
They know the regrets.
They know the nights spent wondering whether they ruined everything.
Yet the God who met Moses in the wilderness still meets people today.
Not because they earned another chance.
Not because they deserve restoration.
But because grace remains one of the defining characteristics of God's kingdom.
The Greek word χάρις (charis), translated "grace," refers to unearned favor freely given.
Grace does not ignore sin.
Grace conquers sin through redemption.
The cross stands as history's greatest evidence that God can take humanity's worst scandal and transform it into salvation.
The execution of Jesus appeared to be the triumph of evil.
Instead, it became the means through which God reconciled sinners to Himself.
What looked like defeat became victory.
What looked like death became life.
What looked like the end became the beginning.
And perhaps that is exactly where some readers find themselves today.
In a wilderness.
In uncertainty.
In regret.
In a season that feels forgotten.
The story of Moses offers a reminder that can change everything:
God still calls people from deserts.
He still redeems failures.
He still transforms fugitives into deliverers.
He still rewrites stories.
Sit with it.
Be honest.
What wilderness are you walking through?
What failure have you allowed to define you?
What chapter have you mistaken for the ending?
Your testimony may become someone else's lifeline.
The same God who met a fugitive beside a burning bush still walks into wildernesses carrying redemption.
